Featuring an OLED screen, three navigation buttons, an RGB status LED, and a passive buzzer, it allows users to manage reminders, track upcoming deadlines, and receive visual and audible notifications through a compact, interactive device.

### 2026-11-01: # MEMO — Building the Schematic and PCB

**5h**

# MEMO — Building the Schematic and PCB

**October 28+29, 2026**

Today, I started working on my new PCB project, MEMO! The idea behind MEMO was to create a small desktop reminder and information display that I could use in my everyday life. I wanted something that could display reminders and other useful information without having to constantly check my phone.

I decided to build it around the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-C3, since it's compact and has enough GPIO pins to support all the different components. For the interface, I wanted to keep things simple but still interactive. I settled on a small OLED display, three mini push buttons for navigation, and an RGB LED to communicate different statuses through colour. The buttons would allow me to move through menus and select options, while the LED would provide visual notifications.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/8edac11fdf8dbef1c9c3d1933a6ab6f5e2f912863430ca608e165475dfcad7b7.png)

---

### Building the Schematic

I started by opening KiCad and creating a new project. I placed all the components into the schematic, including the XIAO ESP32-C3, OLED connector, three mini push buttons, RGB LED, and three current-limiting resistors.

After placing everything, I began connecting the components and organizing the circuit using power symbols and net labels. I assigned separate GPIO pins to each button and each RGB LED colour channel. I also connected the OLED through I2C using SDA and SCL labels rather than drawing long wires across the entire schematic.

For the buttons, I decided to use the ESP32's internal INPUT_PULLUP configuration. This meant each button could connect directly between its GPIO pin and GND without requiring additional pull-up resistors. For the RGB LED, I added three 330 Ω resistors, one for each colour channel, to limit the current and protect the LED and microcontroller.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/4543f510b5793e29ceaae626d9db54e099f4dabe7afe39fd21d4ae9236daf985.png)

### Troubleshooting the Schematic

Once the schematic was complete, I ran KiCad's Electrical Rules Checker (ERC) to identify any potential problems. One of the errors I encountered was "Input power pin not driven by any output power pins."

At first, I was confused because I had already connected the power symbols throughout the circuit. After looking into the issue, I learned that KiCad distinguishes between power input and power output pins. I thought that I had made some kind of mistake but after a bit of research I realized that it was safe to ignore because the XIAO ESP32-C3 supplies power to the circuit, but KiCad didn't recognize its power pin as an output, resulting in a the error.

Now that I knew the error was okay, ignoring this exception, the schematic passed the ERC and  I was ready to start building the PCB.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/0be8cf2ee179d244483c8dc0acec899f6dd89947a753a52439a9757d5ab4f29e.png)

### Building and Routing the PCB

After finishing the schematic and assigning footprints, I moved into the PCB Editor. I imported all the components and started arranging them on the board. I wanted the layout to be practical and visually organized, so I spent time positioning the XIAO, OLED connector, buttons, resistors, and RGB LED in places that made sense for the final device.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/8f8066f5eecdda8a4f6a79257ab8374aaff587f82d30ab2c9ac40b7aa902b7ba.png)

Once I was happy with the component placement, I started routing the traces. I used the ratsnest connections as a guide to connect the different components according to the schematic. I tried to keep the traces as clean and direct as possible while avoiding unnecessary crossings and making efficient use of the available board space.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/e44f2d892c862690e14825b6574d757ad8814d219166b83456c4ab2c3bcf79ab.png)

However, my first routing attempt wasn't as clean as I wanted. I ran into several routing conflicts where traces had to pass around other components or existing connections. In particular, some of my connections became difficult to route without creating awkward detours or running into clearance issues. I also encountered a DRC clearance violation, which meant that two copper items were positioned too close together and did not meet the minimum spacing requirements.

Instead of trying to force the existing routes to work, I decided to undo some of my routing and approach the layout again. I adjusted the paths of several traces, changed how they travelled between components, and used the other copper layer where it made sense. This gave me more room to route the connections without creating unnecessary overlaps or violating the clearance rules.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/b7d807d21ecf3bb6a929c53c762d22d30965867d3f6446fc4d521faddcfe5b5d.png)

After rerouting the traces and checking the connections again, I ran the Design Rules Checker (DRC). This time, the board passed without any remaining violations. It was satisfying to see the entire board connected and pass the manufacturing checks.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/d8850fb8ea7cfbaaf6fee1411a64ab5145be80457b94363c383cd4b911c8fe40.png)

---

**TL;DR:** Designed the MEMO concept, built the complete schematic, assigned footprints, positioned all components, routed every trace, resolved ERC and DRC issues, and finished with a PCB that passes DRC.

**Next time:** Review the final PCB design, prepare the manufacturing files, and begin working on the firmware for the OLED display, buttons, and RGB status LED.

### 2026-11-01: # MEMO — Firmware Development Journal

**6h**

# MEMO — Firmware Development Journal

**October 30–31, 2026**

---

# Building the Core Firmware

For this stage of the MEMO project, my main goal was to develop the firmware that would bring the PCB design to life. I worked in Arduino IDE to program the XIAO ESP32-C3 . This involved creating a reminder system, connecting to Wi-Fi to retrieve the current date and time, displaying deadlines on the OLED, and programming the three buttons and RGB LED to provide visual notifications. Throughout the process, I also had to troubleshoot issues with programming logic, pin assignments, time calculations, and button inputs before combining everything into the final firmware.

## October 30 — Building the Core Firmware

### 1. Setting Up Arduino IDE

I started by moving from the completed KiCad PCB design to programming the XIAO ESP32-C3. I set up Arduino IDE and made sure the correct ESP32 board package was installed so that I could compile and upload code for the microcontroller.

I also installed the libraries needed for the OLED display:

- **Adafruit GFX Library** — provides graphics and text-drawing functions.
- **Adafruit SSD1306** — allows the microcontroller to communicate with and control the OLED display.

Before writing the main program, I organized the code into separate sections for the reminder system, Wi-Fi connection, OLED display, button inputs, and RGB LED. This made it easier to troubleshoot each feature individually instead of trying to write everything in one giant block. I also checked that the correct board and libraries were selected before moving on, since missing libraries or an incorrect board configuration could prevent the firmware from compiling.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/bc8a56987d1963c8bf3c5e003b9444a7737cf47ed090ef7ab16b62d4738a87d5.png)

### 2. Creating the Reminder System

I started by making a `Reminder` structure to store the information associated with each reminder. Each reminder needed a title, a year, a month, a day, an hour, a minute, and a completion status.

Then I created an array with four example reminders. Using an array meant I could store multiple reminders without having to create separate variables for each one. I also used `sizeof()` to calculate the number of reminders automatically, which meant I would not have to manually update the reminder count if I added more entries.

Finally, I created a variable called `selectedReminder` to keep track of which reminder was currently being displayed.

One thing I had to account for was making sure that the selected reminder stayed within the boundaries of the array. Since the program would eventually allow users to move between reminders, the index needed to be handled carefully to avoid trying to access an entry that did not exist. I addressed this later when programming the button navigation.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/ca5c91fa9c6421fc57d01e5df7c7754ee481712ae0e740e56c510766e461dd42.png)

### 3. Initializing the OLED Display

Next, I worked on getting the OLED display functioning. I configured the display resolution to 128 × 64 pixels and set its I²C address to `0x3C`.

One important detail was making sure that the I²C pins matched my actual PCB connections. Since I was using a custom pin arrangement, I used `Wire.begin(SDA_PIN, SCL_PIN)` to explicitly assign SDA to D5 and SCL to D4 rather than relying on the default pin configuration. This was important because the default I²C assignments did not match the connections I had chosen in my KiCad schematic.

I also created the `updateDisplay()` function. This function clears the previous screen, sets the text colour and size, and prints the information that MEMO needs to show. Separating the display code into its own function made it easier to refresh the screen whenever the user changed reminders.

I made sure to keep the display dimensions and I²C address consistent throughout the code so that the library would initialize the correct display configuration.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/6c2c3dc30fe296223fc54eb10491e8e6241f00ac3f027256285d0a2a3b83cc26.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/98d601a5374c9b75bf93aa3e8f663fd4dc9d2e60d952e037f10029545f0cf8a6.png)

### 4. Connecting to Wi-Fi and Getting the Current Time

One of the most important features of MEMO is that it needs to know the actual date and time to calculate how close a deadline is. Instead of manually setting the clock, I decided to use Wi-Fi and Network Time Protocol (NTP).

I used the ESP32's built-in Wi-Fi functionality to connect to a wireless network. I left the Wi-Fi name and password as placeholders in the code because I didn't want my personal network credentials being leaked on GitHub. Once connected, the program requests the current time from an internet time server. I also configured the timezone for Toronto using an EST/EDT timezone string so that the clock would account for daylight saving time.

I added a 20-second connection timeout so the program would not remain stuck indefinitely if Wi-Fi was unavailable. This was important because an unsuccessful connection could otherwise prevent the rest of the program from running. If it could not connect, the display would show a waiting-for-time message instead of attempting to display an inaccurate countdown.

I also made sure that the program waited for the time to synchronize after connecting to Wi-Fi, since successfully connecting to a network does not automatically mean that the current time has already been retrieved.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/aa133aad3351501a434b568ec938a2beb2c957448f8599c260bba5c546d3bbae.png)

### 5. Calculating Deadlines

After setting up the clock, I worked on the main functionality of MEMO: calculating how much time remained before a reminder was due.

I created a `getDeadline()` function that converts the date and time stored in a reminder into a format that the ESP32 can calculate with. This involved using the `tm` structure and the `mktime()` function. I had to account for the fact that the C++ time structure uses a different starting point for years and months, so I subtracted 1900 from the year and 1 from the month.

This was an important detail because using the normal calendar values directly would result in incorrect dates being calculated. I also set `tm_isdst` to `-1`, allowing the time conversion function to determine whether daylight saving time applies.

I then used `difftime()` to compare the reminder's deadline with the current time. This allowed the program to determine whether a reminder was overdue, due within 24 hours, or due further in the future.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/21a93aa2cb7bacafdbc6d51a365649467f5b2c368d89a9c09cbd1074cacb7075.png)

---

## October 31 — Adding Interactivity and Completing the Firmware

### 6. Displaying Reminder Status

On the second day, I continued working on the display and focused on making the deadline information easier to understand.

I used `strftime()` to format the current time and date into readable strings. Rather than displaying raw time values, the OLED shows the time in a 12-hour format and the date using the month, day, and year.

I also added different display messages depending on the reminder's status:

- COMPLETED: The reminder has been marked as finished.
- OVERDUE: The deadline has already passed.
- Due in hours and minutes: The deadline is less than 24 hours away.
- Due in days: The deadline is more than 24 hours away.

While organizing these conditions, I had to make sure that the completed status was checked before the deadline calculations were displayed. Otherwise, a reminder that had already been marked as completed could still appear overdue based on its date. Separating these conditions made the displayed status more accurate and easier to understand.

This made the display more useful because I could quickly understand the urgency of each reminder without having to calculate the time remaining myself.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/b77a6d53fcecb19ba8fb0554032053497730e500240618a27a033bdc27927c6f.png)

### 7. Programming the RGB LED

I then added the RGB LED to provide a visual indication of each reminder's status. I created a `setLED()` function that controls the red, green, and blue channels independently.

The LED uses the following colour system:

Colour: Meaning
- Green :More than 24 hours remaining
- Blue : Less than 24 hours remaining
- Red :Reminder is overdue
- Off : Reminder is completed

I also programmed the LED to display blue while the device is waiting for a valid time connection. This gives the user another way to understand what the device is doing without having to read the entire OLED display.

One thing I had to keep consistent was the relationship between the LED's GPIO pin definitions and the conditions controlling each colour. Since each colour is connected to a separate microcontroller pin through its own resistor, I made sure that the setLED() function controlled the correct channel for each colour.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/fefae214b23ab29acd88af67d2cfb6040cff8f2d5be0087ceaf444702023b5ea.png)

### 8. Programming the Three Buttons

The next step was making MEMO interactive. I programmed the three physical push buttons to allow the user to navigate through reminders and mark them as completed.

Each button uses `INPUT_PULLUP`, meaning that the microcontroller normally reads HIGH and reads LOW when the button is pressed. This allowed me to connect each button between its GPIO pin and GND without needing an external pull-up resistor.

I assigned the buttons the following functions:

- UP: Moves to the previous reminder.
- DOWN: Moves to the next reminder.
- SELECT: Marks the selected reminder as completed or changes it back to incomplete.

I also created a `buttonPressed()` function to handle button inputs. Mechanical buttons can produce multiple electrical signals from a single press, which can cause the program to register more than one input. To help prevent this, I added a 200-millisecond debounce interval and made the function wait until the button was released before accepting another press.

Another detail I had to handle was making sure that reminder navigation loops around. For example, pressing UP while viewing the first reminder takes the user to the last reminder, rather than leaving the selection outside the array. I used conditional statements to reset the selected index whenever it moved beyond the valid range.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/6269aedd4e853f43c5e79ec0bb1a748f734e5ceef84f40fcb1aae4551f89fcb7.png)

### 9. Combining the Features and Final Integration

Once the individual features were written, I combined them into the main program. I organized the `setup()` function to initialize the buttons, LED, OLED, and Wi-Fi connection before displaying the first reminder.

I then used the loop() function to continuously check for button presses and refresh the display. Instead of relying on a long delay(), I used millis() to refresh the screen approximately once every second. This provides regular updates to the clock and deadline countdown while keeping the program responsive to button inputs.

Using millis() was particularly useful because a long delay would have interrupted the program's ability to respond to button presses while waiting for the next display update. I also made sure that the display was refreshed after a button press so that the user could immediately see the newly selected reminder or updated completion status.

### 10. Final Compilation and Firmware Completion

After combining the different sections, I compiled the complete firmware in Arduino IDE and checked that the program built successfully. I reviewed the pin definitions to make sure they matched the connections in my KiCad schematic and checked that the reminder information, display functions, LED controls, and button inputs were all integrated into the same program.

The result was Version 1.0 of MEMO's firmware. It includes a reminder system with a real-time clock synchronized through Wi-Fi, an OLED interface, three-button navigation, and RGB LED status indicators.

There are still some limitations that I could improve in a future version. For example, reminders are currently hardcoded into the program, meaning that changing them requires editing and uploading the firmware again. Completed reminders also reset when the device restarts because their status is not saved permanently. However, the current version establishes the main functionality that I originally wanted MEMO to have.

---

## Summary

Over October 30 and 31, I developed the first complete version of MEMO's firmware using Arduino IDE and C++. I programmed the reminder system, Wi-Fi time synchronization, OLED interface, RGB LED notifications, and three-button navigation. Along the way, I worked through several programming challenges involving date calculations, custom pin assignments, and button handling. By the end, the complete firmware compiled successfully and brought together all the features planned for MEMO's first version.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/19c549744846033238a4798f0878f6dc6c9e63f33f9efaa57d9eee8935fe9606.png)

### 2026-11-01: # MEMO — Day 3 Journal: BOM, GitHub README & File Organization

**3.5h**

# MEMO — Day 3 Journal: BOM, GitHub README & File Organization

November 1, 2026

Today, I focused on finishing the documentation for MEMO and preparing the project for its final submission. With the PCB design and firmware completed, I needed to organize the hardware prices, calculate the total project cost, arrange my project files, and create a README for my GitHub repository explaining how everything works.

### 1. Creating the Bill of Materials (BOM)

I started by putting together a complete Bill of Materials containing every component used in the project. I recorded the quantities, suppliers, individual prices, and total costs. One detail I had to account for was the 330 Ω resistors, since I purchased a pack of 20 but only used three on the PCB.

I also calculated the total hardware cost, which came to **$29.15 CAD**, excluding shipping. Finally, I added purchase links so that anyone viewing the project could find the components.

I sourced all of my components from RobotShop, with the exception of the custom PCB, for which I got a quote from JLCPCB.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/1835ffea23e1d6178d4a060354c7bcb00a515c2a8a7666c3e5a124b45270336e.png)

### 2. Organizing the GitHub README

Next, I began building the project's GitHub README. I wanted it to provide a clear overview of MEMO, explain its purpose, and make the technical details easy to understand for anyone visiting the repository.

I organized the README into several sections, including the project summary, key features, hardware components, BOM, PCB design, pin configuration, physical controls, firmware, and setup instructions. I also included a section explaining the current limitations of the project and possible future improvements.

Rather than putting all the information into large paragraphs, I used tables and smaller subsections to make the documentation easier to navigate. This also allowed someone interested in recreating MEMO to quickly find the components, connections, and software requirements.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/f1645a0c7e20524fe1ab67ffe8ff6bd75724a6e5895426ec73ebf51b3a1a38d7.png)

### 3. Adding Technical Documentation

I then worked on documenting the more technical aspects of MEMO. I added tables explaining the GPIO pin assignments for the OLED, RGB LED, and three push buttons. I also included a controls table describing what each button does and an RGB status table showing how different LED colours communicate reminder statuses.

For the firmware section, I explained the main libraries used, how the ESP32-C3 connects to Wi-Fi, and how NTP is used to synchronize the clock. I also documented the process for configuring Wi-Fi credentials before uploading the code.

I made sure to mention the current limitations, particularly that reminders are hardcoded into the firmware and cannot yet be created or edited directly through the device.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/ded6c10b04694fae9501dabb27b2091eaf8eaa67edd8d9acd3967b57df0c8fc5.png)

### 4. Organizing Project Files Using GitHub.dev

Before pushing my final changes, I also needed to organize the files in my GitHub repository. Instead of editing everything through GitHub's regular website interface, I opened the repository using **GitHub.dev**, which provides a browser-based VS Code environment.

This gave me access to a familiar file explorer and editor directly in my browser. I arranged the project files into appropriate folders so that the repository would be easier to navigate. I separated the firmware, KiCad design files, manufacturing files, and other project documentation rather than leaving everything scattered in the root directory.

I also checked that the important files, such as the schematic, PCB layout, Gerber files, BOM, and Arduino firmware, were included. Once the file structure was organized, I reviewed the changes and committed and pushed them to the repository.

This made the repository much cleaner and ensured that someone downloading the project could locate the files they needed without having to search through unrelated documents.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/69205ad9604d165813352ba3fb9f8f9948a93706928cb1fdfb2a09ed13ab50f3.png)

### 5. Finalizing the README

Finally, I reviewed the README to make sure the component information matched the actual hardware and that the documentation accurately reflected the completed firmware. I also added spaces for images of the schematic and PCB layout to make the project easier to visualize.

After checking the formatting, tables, links, and file organization, I pushed the final documentation changes to GitHub.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/916379f54962383c3376bf48b92207ca7a5058abbf1e33659dc8be9ea37f291f.png)

### Summary

Today, I completed the BOM, organized my GitHub repository using GitHub.dev, and finished the README for MEMO. I documented the hardware costs, component sources, PCB connections, controls, and firmware functionality. With the project files arranged and the documentation completed, MEMO's design and development documentation is now ready for submission.
